fabrics.title: How to wash leggings and technical activewear
fabrics.description: How to wash leggings, sports bras and technical activewear: cool washes, no fabric softener, low or no heat, and how to stop odours building up.
fabrics.lead: Stretch knits, bonded seams, elastic fibres and special performance finishes can respond differently to heat, friction, detergent and softeners.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Start with the care tag, not a universal “cold wash only” slogan. Turn inside out when helpful for surface abrasion, separate rough fasteners and check any product-specific detergent instructions.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Heat-sensitive elastic or bonded details can be a reason for low-temperature or no-tumble instructions. However, waterproof shells sometimes specifically benefit from controlled drying when the maker permits it.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not apply one rule to all technical gear. A DWR-treated jacket can have different wash and dryer instructions from compression leggings; Patagonia documents garment-specific drying steps for shells.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Washing technical fabrics
body: Wash soon after use rather than leaving damp kit in a bag, turn items inside out and use a cool or warm wash within the label limit. Close zips and hooks so they do not snag knits.
Skip fabric softener. It coats the fibres, which can reduce wicking and trap odour.

sections.heading: Drying and odour
body: Heat breaks down elastane over time, so air drying or the lowest permitted dryer setting keeps stretch longer.
If odours persist, a detergent made for sportswear or an extra rinse can help, but only within what the care label permits.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from activewear. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to read the label on blended and lined clothes
fabrics.description: How to wash blended, lined and mixed-material clothes: why the care label covers the whole garment and why the most delicate part sets the rules.
fabrics.lead: A finished garment may combine multiple fibres, stretch bands, lining, adhesives, buttons and decorated surfaces. Its care label represents the whole article rather than the main fabric alone.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Use the complete care sequence. A cotton-rich outer fabric does not override a restrictive instruction chosen because of a lining, elastic panel or dyed trim.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Respect the most specific printed drying method and temperature. If there are separate removable pieces with independent tags, care for each according to its own instructions.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Avoid averaging the fibre composition into a guessed wash temperature. A label can be more restrictive than anything suggested by the material percentages.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: The most delicate part sets the rules
body: When a garment combines fibres, the label should reflect the most sensitive component. A polyester shell with a viscose lining, for example, is limited by the lining.
Linings, shoulder pads and fused interfacing can shrink or bubble at different rates from the outer fabric, which is why many tailored pieces are labelled for professional cleaning.

sections.heading: Trims and decorations
body: Sequins, prints, leather patches and glued details often set the limits. Turning the garment inside out and choosing a gentler cycle within the label reduces friction on them.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from blends. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to care for a cashmere sweater
fabrics.description: How to wash a cashmere sweater safely: reading the label, hand washing, drying flat, removing pills and storing knitwear away from moths.
fabrics.lead: Cashmere is a fine animal fibre, and the garment construction can be more vulnerable than its soft feel suggests. A fibre label does not replace the finished garment’s wash instruction.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Inspect the actual wash tub and any printed note. When hand wash is allowed, handle gently and avoid rubbing, twisting or long unattended soaks. If the label prohibits washing, use the permitted professional method instead.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: A washed cashmere knit is generally best supported flat and carefully reshaped; do not assume tumble drying is acceptable. Keep the item away from direct heater contact and check the care tag for shade-drying details.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: The common failure is washing a cashmere knit like an ordinary cotton tee, then lifting it by the shoulders while saturated. Mechanical action and wet stretching can both change the result.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Washing cashmere by hand
body: If the label allows washing, use cool water and a detergent made for wool or cashmere, and move the garment gently rather than rubbing it.
Do not wring. Roll the sweater in a towel to press out the water, then reshape it and dry it flat away from direct heat.

sections.heading: Pilling and storage
body: Pilling is normal in areas that rub, and a cashmere comb or fabric shaver removes it.
Store cashmere folded rather than hung, and clean it before storage: moth larvae are drawn to keratin fibres, especially soiled ones. Sealed bags or boxes add protection.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from cashmere. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to wash cotton without damaging the garment
fabrics.description: How to wash cotton without shrinking or fading it: reading the tub number, first-wash shrinkage, sorting colours, and lower-heat drying.
fabrics.lead: Cotton is common in everyday clothing, but dye, print, shrinkage control, elastic trims and fabric construction determine the care instructions of the finished item.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Use the temperature shown in the tub as an upper limit, not a goal. For dark or printed garments, separate by colour and turn inside out when the manufacturer advises it.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Do not assume every cotton garment may be tumble dried: cotton tees with elastane, graphics or special finishes may have a crossed dryer symbol.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Bleaching, ironing and drying have separate symbols. A 60°C wash permission does not grant permission to use chlorine bleach or a hot iron.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Shrinkage and the first wash
body: Cotton is most likely to shrink in its first few washes, especially with hot water and high dryer heat. “Pre-shrunk” items have been treated to reduce, not remove, this risk.
A cooler wash and lower dryer heat keep the size more stable.

sections.heading: Colours and ironing
body: Wash new dark or bright cotton separately at first, because loose dye can transfer. White cotton can usually tolerate higher temperatures, but only when the tub number allows it.
Cotton irons most easily while still slightly damp, at the heat the iron symbol permits.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from cotton. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to wash jeans and denim pieces
fabrics.description: How to wash jeans and denim: wash less often, inside out and cool, limit dryer heat, and keep indigo dye from rubbing off onto lighter items.
fabrics.lead: Jeans are often cotton-rich, but dyes, stretch fibres, abrasions and special finishes change how a finished pair should be cleaned.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Read the jeans’ wash mark and any written inside-out or colour-transfer warning. New dark denim may release dye; sort with appropriate dark colours rather than a light or white load.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Follow the dryer mark, especially for stretch denim. Some jeans may permit low tumble drying; others specify line drying. A garment’s elastic recovery can be affected by overheating.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not confuse visible fading from wear with proof that a bleach treatment is allowed. Only the triangle mark tells you whether bleaching is permitted.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Wash less, and gently
body: Jeans rarely need washing after every wear. When you do wash them, button and zip them up, turn them inside out and use a cool wash. This limits fading and abrasion lines.
Air drying avoids the shrinkage and elastane damage that high dryer heat can cause in stretch denim.

sections.heading: Indigo transfer
body: Dark and raw denim can rub indigo dye onto lighter clothes, bags and pale upholstery, especially when new. Wash new pairs separately for the first few washes.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from denim. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to wash linen and manage creasing
fabrics.description: How to wash linen and manage creases: gentle spins, line drying, ironing while damp, and why linen gets softer the more it is washed.
fabrics.lead: Linen fibres can withstand many common domestic processes, but a finished linen piece may have restrictive dyes, tailoring, lining or shrinkage-sensitive finishes.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Choose the printed tub temperature and cycle rather than a generic “hot wash linen” rule. New colours and mixed linen garments may need a gentler approach than a plain white household linen article.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Follow the square: some linen articles are line dried while others are suitable for tumble drying. Promptly removing the article from the washer can reduce creasing, but does not override the drying mark.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: A three-dot iron setting is only permitted if the iron mark actually shows it. Do not assume maximum ironing heat from the fibre name alone.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Washing and creasing
body: Linen generally softens and becomes more comfortable with each wash. A gentle cycle with a lower spin speed and a load that is not too full reduces deep creases.
Remove it promptly from the machine and shake it out.

sections.heading: Drying and ironing
body: Line drying keeps linen fresher and reduces shrinkage risk compared with high dryer heat. For a crisp finish, iron while slightly damp at the heat the label allows.
Many people accept some creasing as part of linen’s look.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from linen. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to care for polyester and nylon blends
fabrics.description: How to wash polyester and nylon: low heat to avoid glazing or melting, beating trapped odours, reducing static, and cutting microfibre shedding.
fabrics.lead: Polyester and nylon are synthetic fibres used in many garments, but surface finishes, insulation, bonded seams and decorative elements determine the finished-item instructions.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Read the wash tub for the actual temperature and movement limit. Separate lint-shedding towels from smooth synthetics where practical, and respect any written detergent restrictions.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Use the drying mark rather than assuming synthetics can tolerate a hot dryer. Some pieces allow low heat while others need air drying to protect their construction.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not set an iron to the cotton or linen setting because the garment appears thick. Check the iron dots and use a cloth when appropriate.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Heat is the main risk
body: Synthetic fibres soften at high temperatures, so a hot iron can leave shiny glazed patches or even melt the fabric. Use the lowest iron setting the label allows, ideally with a pressing cloth.
Cool or warm washes and low dryer heat also reduce permanent creasing.

sections.heading: Odour, static and shedding
body: Polyester holds on to body oils more than cotton, so sportswear can keep odours. Washing soon after wear helps.
Avoid over-drying to reduce static. Full loads, cooler washes and shorter cycles reduce the number of microfibres released.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from polyester. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

fabrics.title: How to wash silk clothing without guessing
fabrics.description: How to wash silk without damage: when hand washing is allowed, pH-neutral detergent, no wringing, drying out of the sun and low-heat ironing.
fabrics.lead: Silk garments may include delicate dyes, surface finishes, lining and trims. Two pure-silk pieces can have very different safe-care labels.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Read both the wash permission and professional circle. If hand washing is explicitly allowed, use the specified temperature and gentle handling; if the tub is crossed, do not improvise with a cold rinse.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Avoid wringing silk. If the square includes a shade mark, use a shaded drying area; natural-dry directions may differ for dresses, scarves and structured garments.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not infer bleach or ironing permission from fibre content. The triangle and iron marks are independent decisions, and many silk dyes or treatments can be affected by water or steam.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: When hand washing is allowed
body: If the label permits washing, use cool water and a gentle, pH-neutral detergent suitable for silk, and keep the soak short. Avoid detergents with protease enzymes, which can attack protein fibres.
Press the water out in a towel instead of wringing.

sections.heading: Drying and ironing silk
body: Dry silk away from direct sunlight, because UV light can yellow and weaken it. Iron on a low setting on the reverse side while the fabric is slightly damp.
Some silks show water marks. These pieces are usually labelled for professional cleaning.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from silk. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

sections.heading: Source notes and publication editions

fabrics.title: How to wash viscose and rayon garments
fabrics.description: How to wash viscose and rayon: why it weakens when wet, gentle cool washing, minimal spin, reshaping and drying, and the shrinkage risk.
fabrics.lead: Viscose and rayon can have reduced dimensional stability while wet, depending on yarn construction, finishing and blends. Not every rayon article is machine washable.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: If the tub permits a mild wash, match the cycle precisely and do not twist or stretch the wet article. Where the wash mark is crossed, follow the professional-care instructions instead.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Respect a flat-dry or line-dry specification. Handle saturated garments carefully to prevent unwanted lengthening or distortion while the fibre is wet.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: The mistake is assuming an item is robust because it feels like cotton. Consult its finished garment care label and professional cleaning circle.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Why viscose needs extra care when wet
body: Viscose and rayon lose a large share of their strength when wet, so twisting, wringing and fast spins can stretch or distort them.
Where washing is permitted, a cool, gentle cycle or hand washing with minimal spin is the safer choice.

sections.heading: Drying and ironing
body: Reshape the garment and dry it flat or on a padded hanger, away from direct heat. Viscose can shrink noticeably with heat, so avoid the dryer unless the label allows it.
Iron on the reverse at the temperature the label permits, while slightly damp.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from viscose. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

sections.heading: Source notes and publication editions

fabrics.title: How to wash wool without losing its shape
fabrics.description: How to wash wool without shrinking it: wool programmes, enzyme-free detergent, flat drying, and keeping clean knits safe from moths.
fabrics.lead: Wool can felt or change shape when moisture, friction and heat combine. Some finished wool garments are machine-washable, while others are hand-wash or professional-care only.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Check for a wool- or very-mild-cycle label, not merely the word “wool” on the composition tag. Washable wool can often use a dedicated wool program when the label allows it; tailored, lined or embellished pieces may need a different process.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: For a wet sweater, support its full weight and reshape it on a pale, lint-free towel. Woolmark recommends flat drying knitwear unless the item specifically permits tumble drying; some approved wool items do permit a suitable low-heat dryer.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Avoid treating all wool as dry-clean-only or all wool as machine-washable. Those are both unsafe shortcuts. Strong agitation and hanging a heavy wet knit can cause problems even when the water temperature is low.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Machine wool programmes and detergent
body: Many machines have a wool programme with low agitation and cool water, designed for items labelled machine-washable.
Use a detergent formulated for wool. Ordinary biological detergents can contain protease enzymes that break down wool’s protein fibres.

sections.heading: Storage and moths
body: Clean wool before storing it, because moth larvae are attracted to keratin fibres and especially to soiled garments. Store clean, dry knitwear folded in a closed drawer, box or bag, and check stored items periodically.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from wool. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

guides.title: Bleach symbols explained: triangle, lines and cross
guides.description: Empty triangle, triangle with two lines or a crossed triangle: what each bleach symbol allows, chlorine vs oxygen bleach, and how to test first.
guides.lead: An empty triangle, a triangle with two lines, and a crossed triangle give three different permissions. The small difference determines whether chlorine bleach, oxygen bleach or no bleach is permitted.

sections.heading: Empty triangle: bleach when appropriate
body: Both chlorine and oxygen bleaching are permitted by the symbol, but the product still must be used correctly. “Allowed” does not mean “required.”

sections.heading: Two diagonal lines: non-chlorine only
body: Choose an oxygen/non-chlorine product when bleaching is needed. Do not confuse a detergent’s marketing label with its actual ingredients.

sections.heading: Crossed triangle: none
body: Avoid all bleaching agents, including oxygen bleach and bleach-containing detergent additives.

sections.heading: Other symbols still apply
body: A bleach-permitted item can still have a restrictive washing temperature or drying method. Read the complete care label.

sections.heading: Chlorine bleach versus oxygen bleach
body: Chlorine bleach (sodium hypochlorite) is a strong oxidiser. It whitens and disinfects, but it strips many dyes and weakens protein fibres such as wool and silk, as well as elastane.

Oxygen bleaches are based on hydrogen peroxide or sodium percarbonate. They are gentler on most colours, but they can still lighten some dyes. Neither type is automatically safe on wool or silk: check the product label as well as the garment.

sections.heading: Test before you bleach
body: Even when the triangle permits bleach, test colourfastness on a hidden area such as an inside seam. Apply the solution at the strength the product directs, wait a minute, then blot with a white cloth. Any colour change or transfer means the item should not be bleached.
Never mix chlorine bleach with ammonia, acids or other cleaners: the combination releases toxic gases.

sections.heading: Stain removers and older labels
body: Many stain removers and “colour-safe” boosters contain oxygen bleach. On an item with a crossed triangle, avoid them unless the garment maker says otherwise.
Some older labels show “Cl” inside the triangle. That was an earlier way of saying chlorine bleach is allowed.

sections.heading: No made-up test results.
body: Care advice here summarizes published sources. We have not performed garment-specific laboratory tests. A damaged item may need professional assessment.

guides.title: My black clothes faded: can the colour come back?
guides.description: Why black clothes fade or turn grey, how to tell dye loss from detergent residue, and the washing habits that keep dark colours deeper for longer.
guides.lead: Colour loss may come from dye transfer, surface abrasion, detergent chemistry or light. If dye has actually left the fabric, an ordinary wash usually cannot restore the original colour.

sections.heading: Check whether it is residue or dye loss
body: A powdery film may be detergent or lint; uneven pale patches may indicate chemical damage or abrasion. Do not add bleach to “brighten” dark clothing.

sections.heading: Avoid further colour damage
body: Sort darks from lights, follow the care-label temperature and bleach triangle, and avoid direct sun if the drying symbol specifies shade.

sections.heading: Be careful with dyeing
body: Home recolouring can stain stitching, elastics or trims differently, and may not be suitable for all fibre blends. Follow dye product and garment instructions before attempting it.

sections.heading: Prevent future fading
body: Read the laundry and drying marks as one set. The bleach triangle and corner-shade slash often explain decisions that temperature alone cannot.

sections.heading: Why black fades faster than other colours
body: Black garments lose depth through friction in the drum, repeated washing, sunlight and heat. The loss is visible sooner on black than on mid-tones, and cotton blacks usually fade faster than polyester blacks because the dyes bond to the fibre differently.

sections.heading: Habits that keep dark colours deeper
body: Turn garments inside out, wash at the lowest temperature the label allows, choose a shorter cycle, and avoid overloading the drum so items rub less.

A detergent made for dark colours and a correct dose help, because excess detergent and hard-water deposits can leave a grey film that looks like fading. Dry out of direct sunlight and avoid high dryer heat.

sections.heading: Residue or real dye loss?
body: If the greyness is patchy, feels stiff or shows white streaks along folds, it is often residue. An extra rinse with no detergent may improve it. Even, all-over lightening, especially on seams and edges, points to real dye loss, which washing cannot reverse.

sections.heading: No made-up test results.
body: Care advice here summarizes published sources. We have not performed garment-specific laboratory tests. A damaged item may need professional assessment.

guides.title: How to read laundry care symbols in order
guides.description: Read laundry care symbols in order: wash tub, bleach triangle, drying square, iron and professional-care circle, with a worked example.
guides.lead: Start with the wash tub, then check bleach, drying, ironing and the professional-care circle. Each mark controls a different treatment, and an absent mark does not automatically authorize it.

sections.heading: 1. Read the sequence, not just one mark
body: International labels normally follow washing, bleaching, drying, ironing and professional care. The precise sequence helps prevent mixing a crossed dryer with a crossed wash tub.

sections.heading: 2. Read the modifiers
body: Numbers in a tub are maximum wash temperatures. One line under a symbol requests a milder process; two lines call for a very mild process. Dryer dots and iron dots have their own meanings.

sections.heading: 3. Check the finished article
body: The label accounts for the entire garment, including finishes, attached decoration and lining. Fibre composition alone cannot determine whether tumbling or bleaching is allowed.

sections.heading: 4. If a mark is missing or unreadable
body: Leave it unknown and consult the other written instructions or manufacturer. Our decoder does not infer permission from an empty slot.

sections.heading: The five symbol families at a glance
body: Wash tub: washing. Triangle: bleaching. Square: drying, where a circle inside the square means tumble drying. Iron: ironing. Circle: professional cleaning.
In the professional-care circle, the letters P and F refer to dry-cleaning solvents and W means professional wet cleaning. A cross through any symbol means that treatment should not be used.

sections.heading: Dots and lines on the dryer and iron
body: Inside the tumble-dry symbol, one dot means low heat and two dots normal heat. In the natural-drying square, a vertical line means line dry, three vertical lines mean drip dry and a horizontal line means dry flat. A diagonal line in the corner means dry in the shade.
On the iron, more dots allow more heat; see the ISO vs ASTM guide for how the temperatures differ between editions. Crossed lines under the iron mean no steam.

sections.heading: A worked example
body: Suppose a tag shows a tub with 30 and one bar, a crossed triangle, a tumble-dry square with one dot, an iron with one dot and a circle with P.
Read in order, that means: machine wash at up to 30°C on a mild cycle, no bleach, tumble dry on low heat, iron on the lowest setting, and professional dry cleaning is allowed.

sections.heading: Where to find the label
body: Care labels are usually sewn into a side seam or the back of the neck, and some garments have several panels. Printed words such as “wash dark colours separately” add to the symbols, so read both.

sections.heading: No made-up test results.
body: Care advice here summarizes published sources. We have not performed garment-specific laboratory tests. A damaged item may need professional assessment.

guides.title: ISO vs ASTM care symbols: what actually differs?
guides.description: How international ISO 3758 care symbols differ from the U.S. ASTM convention, why ironing temperatures vary by edition, and which to use.
guides.lead: ISO 3758:2023 is the international standard. The U.S. has its own longstanding ASTM-based symbol convention; the public FTC-hosted chart reflects a historical edition, not the full 2025 ASTM standard.

sections.heading: Temperature inside the wash tub
body: International ISO tubs usually show a temperature number such as 30 or 40. The U.S. reference includes dot-based wash-temperature symbols. Never convert them by guesswork.

sections.heading: Ironing temperatures have changed
body: Current public ISO 2023 guides describe low, medium and high limits of 120°C, 160°C and 210°C. Older U.S. references commonly use 110°C, 150°C and 200°C. The decoder keeps these editions separate.

sections.heading: Current standard versus historical public chart
body: ASTM lists D5489-25 as active. Its licensed full content is not bundled here; we do not claim a historical FTC chart represents that entire new guide.

sections.heading: How to choose in the decoder
body: Use ISO for a number-in-tub international tag and the U.S. historical guide for a U.S. dot-based tag when it matches. When uncertain, compare against the original manufacturer’s instructions.

sections.heading: Why labels differ between markets
body: In Europe the familiar symbols come from ISO 3758 and are promoted by GINETEX. In the United States, the FTC Care Labeling Rule requires care instructions on most textile clothing and allows ASTM symbols in place of words. Canada uses its own standard, which is aligned with the ISO symbols.
A garment made for several markets may carry more than one convention, so check which system a tag follows before decoding it.

sections.heading: The practical rule
body: If the wash tub contains a number, read it as an ISO temperature in degrees Celsius. If it contains dots, use the U.S. reference. When the two disagree on the same garment, follow the stricter instruction.

guides.title: Missing or unreadable laundry symbols: what to do
guides.description: Care label missing or faded? Why a blank slot is not permission, the lowest-risk way to clean an unlabelled item, and what labelling rules require.
guides.lead: A missing symbol is not proof that a treatment is allowed. When a label is partly faded or cut off, use written maker instructions, garment information and professional advice rather than reconstructing permissions from guesses.

sections.heading: Look for more than one label
body: Some garments have a side-seam care label and a separate composition label. Check removable components and manufacturer-provided care instructions.

sections.heading: Do not fill in invisible marks
body: If the dryer symbol is absent or too damaged to read, mark machine drying as unknown. The decoder intentionally leaves treatment categories incomplete.

sections.heading: Use photo magnification, not unsupported auto-recognition
body: A zoomed image may help you distinguish an underline, dot or diagonal stroke. Camera quality and folds can produce misleading shapes, so the final selection must be confirmed manually.

sections.heading: Ask for verified care details
body: For a valuable or unusual item, contact the manufacturer or a textile-care professional with a readable photo of the complete tag.

sections.heading: The lowest-risk way to clean an unlabelled item
body: If you have to clean it before you can confirm the care, choose the gentlest treatment: cool hand washing or a delicate cycle with mild detergent, no bleach, no tumble drying, and drying flat or on a line out of direct sun.
Test on a hidden area first. This lowers the risk but does not guarantee the result, and structured, lined or embellished pieces are better taken to a professional cleaner.

sections.heading: What labelling rules require
body: In the United States, the FTC Care Labeling Rule requires a permanent care label on most textile clothing. In the European Union, fibre composition labelling is mandatory, but care symbols are voluntary.
If a new garment arrived without care information, the seller or brand is the best place to ask, and it is worth keeping their written answer.

guides.title: I shrank a sweater: what can I do now?
guides.description: Shrunk a sweater? Tell felting from relaxation shrinkage, what gentle reshaping can and cannot recover, and how to stop it happening again.
guides.lead: First identify whether the sweater felted or merely dried out of shape. Some distortion may respond to careful professional reshaping; felting is often not fully reversible, so avoid promised “miracle fixes.”

sections.heading: Stop the damaging treatment
body: Do not run a second hot wash or tumble dry in an attempt to loosen fibres. Check the label and keep the sweater away from direct heat while deciding what to do.

sections.heading: Assess the change
body: A compact, dense surface suggests felting after heat and agitation. A garment stretched in one direction may have changed shape during wet hanging; that is a different problem.

sections.heading: Consider cautious reshaping only when permitted
body: If the garment may be wetted, gentle flat reshaping by hand may help some distortion. Do not use force or household chemicals based on viral tricks; consider a textile-care specialist for valuable items.

sections.heading: Prevent a repeat
body: Check the wash tub for very-mild and hand-wash marks, and the square for flat drying and no-tumble restrictions. Woolmark advises flat drying many wet wool sweaters.

sections.heading: Why wool shrinks: felting
body: Wool fibres have tiny overlapping scales. With heat, moisture and agitation together, the scales lock into each other and the fabric tightens. This is felting, and it is largely permanent.
Cotton and many other fibres shrink differently. Tension added during manufacturing relaxes in water and heat, which shortens the fabric. That change is sometimes partly recoverable.

sections.heading: Gentle reshaping: what to expect
body: A widely shared method is to soak the item in lukewarm water with a little hair conditioner or a wool product to relax the fibres, then press out the water and ease the knit back towards its shape while it dries flat.
It can recover some size from a knit that has tightened. It cannot undo heavy felting, so stretch slowly and stop if seams strain. Do not use it on items labelled dry-clean only.

guides.title: 30°C, 40°C, 60°C: what the wash numbers mean
guides.description: What 30°C, 40°C and 60°C mean in the wash tub symbol, what the bars underneath change, and how to match the label to your machine programme.
guides.lead: The number in an international washing tub is the maximum permissible water temperature for that garment and cycle. You may choose a cooler wash, but that does not remove any gentle-cycle restriction.

sections.heading: 30°C and 40°C are not universal defaults
body: Many everyday garments use these limits, but colourfastness, trims and finishes still matter. A bar under the tub reduces agitation; it does not alter the numeric maximum.

sections.heading: 60°C and hotter need a specific label
body: Some household items allow higher temperatures, but never infer this from their cotton content. Read the tub and any printed text on the actual item.

sections.heading: Cooler is not always equally effective
body: A lower setting may clean less effectively for some soils or hygiene needs. Follow detergent and appliance directions and use an allowed temperature rather than exceeding the label.

sections.heading: U.S. dots are a separate reference
body: The historical U.S. chart includes numbered dot levels in the wash tub. Use the corresponding reference system rather than treating dots as an ISO temperature number.

sections.heading: What the common numbers usually suit
body: When the label allows it, 30°C suits lightly soiled everyday items, delicate colours and many synthetics. 40°C covers most everyday cotton and mixed loads.
60°C is used for towels, bedding and underwear where heavier soil or hygiene matters. 95°C is a boil wash reserved for items that are labelled for it, typically white cotton or linen.

sections.heading: The bars and hand under the tub
body: No bar means a normal process. One bar means a mild process with less agitation, often the synthetics or easy-care programme. Two bars mean a very mild process, such as a wool or delicates programme.
A hand in the tub means hand wash only. A crossed tub means do not wash with water at home.

sections.heading: Matching the label to your machine
body: Choose a programme and temperature at or below the tub number and with no more agitation than the bars allow. Heating the water accounts for most of a washing machine’s energy use, so a lower allowed temperature also saves energy.
Eco programmes often run longer at lower temperatures to compensate.

guides.title: How to wash a weighted blanket without damaging it
guides.description: Weighted blankets are heavy when wet. Check the label and your machine's capacity, wash the cover separately, and dry the insert gently.
guides.lead: A weighted blanket can weigh several times more once it is soaked, and many have a removable cover and a bead-filled insert with different care rules. Read both labels before anything goes in the drum.

sections.heading: Check the weight against your machine
body: Compare the blanket's dry weight with your washing machine's maximum load. Water adds a lot of weight, and an overloaded drum can strain the machine and leave the blanket poorly rinsed.
If it is too heavy for your machine, a large-capacity machine at a laundromat or hand washing in a bathtub are the usual alternatives.

sections.heading: Wash the cover on its own
body: If the blanket has a removable cover, unzip it and wash it according to its own label, usually like a duvet cover. Covers need washing far more often than the weighted insert.

sections.heading: Washing the insert
body: Only machine-wash the insert if its label allows it. Use a gentle cycle, the temperature on the label and a mild detergent, with no bleach or fabric softener.
Glass-bead and plastic-pellet fillings can shift, so a slow spin helps keep them evenly spread.

sections.heading: Drying
body: Follow the drying symbol. Many inserts must be air-dried flat or over several lines to spread the weight; tumble-dry only on the heat the label allows, and make sure the centre is fully dry before use.

guides.title: How to wash a baseball cap or hat
guides.description: How to wash a cap without ruining its shape: check the label and brim, hand wash in cool water, clean the sweatband, and air-dry on a form.
guides.lead: Caps combine fabric, a stiffened front panel and a brim insert. The structure, not just the fabric, decides how it can be washed, so hand washing is usually the safest choice.

sections.heading: Check the label and the brim
body: Look for a care label inside. Older caps can have cardboard in the brim, which warps when soaked; most modern caps use plastic. If you can't tell, spot clean rather than submerging.

sections.heading: Hand wash gently
body: Fill a basin with cool water and a little mild detergent. Clean the cap with a soft brush or cloth, paying attention to the sweatband, then rinse in clean water.

sections.heading: Spot clean what you can't soak
body: For wool caps, embroidery or leather straps, dab only the dirty area with a damp cloth and mild detergent, then blot with a clean damp cloth.

sections.heading: Dry it in shape
body: Press out water with a towel and air-dry the cap over a rounded form, such as a bowl or rolled towel, away from direct heat. Don't use a tumble dryer.

guides.title: How to wash pillows by fill type
guides.description: Can you wash your pillows? Polyester and down pillows often can; memory foam and latex usually can't. How to tell, wash and dry each type fully.
guides.lead: Whether a pillow can go in the washing machine depends on its fill, so start with the label. Getting it completely dry afterwards matters as much as the wash.

sections.heading: Know the fill
body: Polyester fibrefill and down or feather pillows are often machine-washable when the label allows it. Memory foam and latex pillows are usually not: they can tear or break apart when soaked.

sections.heading: Machine-washable pillows
body: Wash two pillows together to balance the drum, on a gentle cycle at the label's temperature with a small amount of detergent. An extra rinse and spin removes more soap and water.

sections.heading: Foam and latex pillows
body: Remove and wash the cover separately. Spot clean the foam with a damp cloth and mild detergent, then let it air out fully before replacing the cover.

sections.heading: Dry completely
body: Tumble-dry on low heat if the label allows, with dryer balls to stop the fill clumping, and check the centre is dry before use. Damp fill can smell and grow mould.

guides.title: How to wash a backpack
guides.description: How to clean a backpack safely: empty it, check the label, hand wash with mild detergent and a soft brush, and air-dry upside down with pockets open.
guides.lead: Backpacks often have coated fabrics, padding, leather trim and sometimes a frame. Hand washing is the safest approach unless the maker says machine washing is fine.

sections.heading: Empty and prepare it
body: Empty every pocket, shake out crumbs, and vacuum the seams. Remove any detachable frame, hip belt or stiffening sheet.

sections.heading: Check the label
body: Some backpacks say machine-washable on a gentle cycle in cold water; others say hand wash or spot clean only. Leather trims and waterproof coatings usually rule out machine washing.

sections.heading: Hand wash
body: Soak it in cool water with a little mild detergent, scrub dirty areas with a soft brush, and rinse until the water runs clear. Avoid harsh detergents that can strip water-repellent coatings.

sections.heading: Dry it fully
body: Hang it upside down with all pockets open so water drains, away from direct heat. Don't tumble-dry: heat can damage coatings, foam and zips.

guides.title: How to wash a comforter or duvet
guides.description: How to wash a comforter at home: check that it fits your machine, use a gentle cycle and an extra rinse, then dry it fully on low heat.
guides.lead: A comforter needs space to move in the drum to come out clean and rinse properly. If it doesn't fit comfortably, a larger machine or a professional cleaner is the better option.

sections.heading: Check the label and the size
body: Read the care label for washing and drying limits. The comforter should fit loosely in the drum; a tightly packed one won't rinse properly and can strain the machine.

sections.heading: Choose the right machine
body: A front-loader or a top-loader without a central agitator is gentler on the stitching and fill.

sections.heading: Wash gently
body: Use a gentle cycle at the label's temperature, a small amount of mild detergent (a down wash for down-filled comforters), and an extra rinse.

sections.heading: Dry thoroughly
body: Tumble-dry on low heat with dryer balls, taking it out every so often to break up clumps. Down can take several cycles; keep going until no damp pockets remain.

guides.title: How to wash sneakers and canvas shoes
guides.description: How to wash shoes without damaging them: remove laces and insoles, scrub by hand, machine wash only canvas or fabric pairs the maker allows, and air-dry.
guides.lead: Shoes are held together by glues and shaped materials that don't like heat. Material decides the method: canvas and fabric are often washable, leather and suede are not.

sections.heading: Prepare the shoes
body: Remove the laces and insoles, knock off loose dirt, and brush away dried mud.

sections.heading: Hand wash first
body: Scrub the uppers and soles with a soft brush, mild soap and warm water. Wash laces separately by hand or in a mesh bag.

sections.heading: Machine washing canvas and fabric shoes
body: Only if the maker allows it: put the shoes in a mesh laundry bag with a couple of towels to cushion them, and use a gentle, cold cycle. Don't machine-wash leather, suede or shoes with glued-on parts that are already lifting.

sections.heading: Dry without heat
body: Stuff the shoes with paper to hold their shape and let them air-dry away from direct heat. A tumble dryer or radiator can melt glue and shrink materials.

guides.title: How to wash a down jacket
guides.description: How to wash a down or puffer jacket at home: down-specific wash, a gentle cycle and an extra rinse, then a long low-heat tumble dry until fully dry.
guides.lead: Down clumps when wet and only regains its loft when completely dry. Washing is gentle; the drying is where most of the care goes. Always check the label first, as some jackets must be professionally cleaned.

sections.heading: Check the label and prepare
body: Confirm the jacket is washable. Empty the pockets, close every zip and Velcro tab, and loosen any drawcords.

sections.heading: Wash gently
body: Use a front-loader or a top-loader without an agitator, a down-specific wash, the label's temperature and a gentle cycle. Add an extra rinse to remove all detergent.

sections.heading: Dry fully on low heat
body: Tumble-dry on low heat with dryer balls to break up clumps, taking the jacket out every so often to tease apart any lumps. It can take several hours. Damp down smells and loses warmth.

sections.heading: Things to avoid
body: Skip fabric softener and regular detergent, which can coat the down and reduce loft. Don't wring the jacket.

guides.title: How to wash towels so they stay soft and absorbent
guides.description: How to wash towels: wash new ones first, use the right temperature and less detergent, skip fabric softener, and dry them fully to avoid musty smells.
guides.lead: Towels lose absorbency when detergent and softener build up in the loops, and they smell musty when they stay damp. Most of the fix is using less product and drying them fully.

sections.heading: Wash new towels first
body: New towels often carry finishes and loose dye. Wash them before first use, separately from other colours.

sections.heading: Temperature and detergent
body: Use the warmest temperature the care label allows; cotton towels often tolerate 40–60°C. Use the recommended dose of detergent, not more, so it rinses out fully.

sections.heading: Skip fabric softener
body: Softener coats the cotton loops and reduces absorbency. Wool dryer balls in the dryer can help keep towels fluffy instead.

sections.heading: Dry them completely
body: Shake towels out before drying, then tumble-dry or line-dry until fully dry. Don't leave damp towels in the machine or in a pile.
